newsitem.title: USA: U.S. bomb trial judge tries to pin down juror.
newsitem.headline: U.S. bomb trial judge tries to pin down juror.

text.p: The judge and attorneys in the Oklahoma City bombing trial tried to pin down a potential juror Monday on whether she would be able to vote for the death penalty despite her strong views against it.

The young cosmetics saleswoman, who at first said capital punishment was never justified, insisted under questioning by a defence attorney that she would be able to set aside her views and consider the death penalty if Timothy McVeigh was found guilty of the bombing.

Another potential juror, a schoolteacher from a remote mountain town, said she was concerned about living alone in a big city like Denver if chosen to serve on the jury. She also suggested that the elaborate security precautions surrounding the trial had also caused her some worry.
"The security arrangements (put in place for the jurors) let me know that you or the courts or someone thinks safety is an issue," she said.

Death penalty concerns dominated the start of the second week of jury selection in the trial of McVeigh, a 28-year-old Gulf War veteran accused of blowing up the Alfred P. Murrah federal building on April 19, 1995, killing 168 people and injuring hundreds. He has pleaded not guilty.
McVeigh could face the death penalty if convicted. Jury candidates are disqualified in capital cases if they could not vote for execution under any circumstances.

The first potential juror questioned, a cosmetics saleswoman only three years out of high school, initially stood by her view that the death penalty was never justified. "I don't feel any human being has the right to judge somebody. That's left up to a higher being," she said.
But, questioned by chief defence attorney Stephen Jones, she said she would be willing to set aside her personal view and consider the death penalty if McVeigh is convicted.

The school teacher said she was concerned about "being in Denver by myself" if selected as one of the 12 jurors. "Safety is a concern -- there's a reason I like living in a small town," the woman, who like other potential jurors was not identified by name, told the court.
She said she lived so far away that she would have to move to the Denver area for the trial, which is expected to last up to four months. She was also concerned about the welfare of her two dogs.

Tight security has been imposed at the federal courthouse in Denver, which was protected by concrete barricades, metal detectors and a large police force. The court is taking strict precautions to keep the identities of potential jurors secret, refering to them only by numbers and shielding them from public view with a screen.
By mid-day Monday, 34 candidates had been interviewed in more than five days of laborious questioning. The judge and opposing attorneys were trying to whittle down a pool of around 350 people to 64.
Each side could then challenge 23 jurors without giving a reason before settling on 12 jurors and six alternates. The process was expected to take up to four weeks.
McVeigh sat next to his lawyers in the courtroom paying close attention to the questioning.

Apart from their views on the death penalty and their exposure to pre-trial publicity, the lawyers were probing the jury candidates to see if they were likely to accept the government's case or be open to defence theories.
McVeigh was accused of planning the bombing with former Army buddy Terry Nichols, who will be tried separately.
